title: When Advocacy Crosses the Line
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post warns that passionate advocacy, a real leadership strength, can slip into condescension without the speaker noticing. The author names three ways advocates unintentionally belittle others: patronizing statements that imply superiority, discounting statements that dismiss others' views, and countering statements that push opposition further than needed. Each is illustrated with sample phrases. The central point is that condescension is rarely deliberate, so leaders must stay on guard precisely when they feel most strongly about what they believe.
points: Condescension is usually unintentional, born of conviction and self-belief rather than malice.
Three patterns to avoid: patronizing, discounting, and countering statements.
Concrete sample phrases help leaders recognize these habits in their own speech.
The risk is highest when the advocate feels most strongly about their position.
quotes: Persuasive advocates believe deeply in what they are proposing and marshal passion and enthusiasm to make their case. Passion sells, but it can sometimes go too far.

Without meaning to, strong and passionate advocates sometimes cross the line and say things others find demeaning. In their desire to express themselves with conviction, they can make others feel less than, small, or unimportant.
Condescension is rarely done on purpose. Advocates normally don’t realize they are saying disrespectful things but get caught up in their passion and self-belief.

Discounting statements: These are statements that project incredulity and a general disregard for the opinions of others. For example, “You don’t know what you’re talking about,” or “You need to do your homework.” Such statements drip with condescension.
Condescension can leak out without intention. Strong advocacy can sometimes bring out the worst in what we say to others. Statements clothed in condescension are off-putting and unnecessary.
